classification.difficultyReason: Identify each argument as a power of its base and read off the exponent, including the zero exponent for 1.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly evaluate logarithms of integer powers. The source explicitly refers to Example 2; no logarithm-law expansion or equation-solving extension is required.
questions.methodNote: Express the argument as a power of the logarithm's base, then identify the exponent, following Example 2 Method 1 on PDF page 4. For an argument of 1, use the zero power or Logarithmic Law 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate logarithms by recognising non-negative integer powers of their bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate logarithms by expressing reciprocal fractions and decimals as negative integer powers of their bases.

questions.mappingNote: The definition on page 2 and the reciprocal examples 2e–f on page 4 directly support all eight negative-index evaluations. Pages 3 and 5 were inspected for the surrounding logarithm laws and examples.
questions.methodNote: Express each argument as a power of its logarithm base, then read off the exponent, following Example 2 Method 1 on PDF page 4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate logarithms by expressing reciprocal fractions and decimals as negative integer powers of their bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite products, radicals and a reciprocal as powers of the logarithm base, then evaluate exactly.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e combine an integer power with a square root; f also uses a reciprocal; g uses a cube root; h rewrites the square root as a power of 8. The logarithm definition on page 2 and Example 2 support every evaluation.
questions.methodNote: Express the argument as a power of the logarithm base and read off its exponent, following Example 2 Method 1 on PDF page 4. Fractional powers represent radicals; negative powers represent reciprocals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rewrite products, radicals and a reciprocal as powers of the logarithm base, then evaluate exactly.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert to exponential form, evaluate the power and, in the shifted arguments, undo an addition or subtraction to isolate x.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f directly use the conversion shown in Example 3a, including reciprocal powers for d and e. Parts g–i use the shifted-argument method of Example 3b. The assessed task is solving logarithmic equations rather than conversion alone.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a logarithm to convert to exponential form, evaluate the power, then isolate x. Example 3a and b on pages 4–5 explicitly model these steps.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert logarithmic equations to exponential form, evaluate integer powers and isolate a shifted argument.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the unknown base into a power equation, take the appropriate root and retain the positive base; part b also requires simplifying a fractional exponent.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess an unknown logarithm base. Parts a, c, d, e and f give integer bases; part b additionally uses fractional indices to obtain the exact base. Page 2 supplies the definition and base restrictions.
questions.methodNote: Convert logarithmic form to exponential form, express the numerical value as a power and choose the positive base, as demonstrated in Example 3c, d on pages 4–5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert logarithmic equations to exponential form and find the positive base, including one fractional-index result.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly convert six logarithmic statements to exponential form, including negative and fractional exponents and pronumerals.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses index–log conversion. Retain the given base, argument and exponent, including the negative exponent in c and fractional exponent in d; e and f reverse the pronumeral conversions in Example 4.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition log_a y=x exactly when a^x=y. Page 2 defines this correspondence; pages 3–4 demonstrate numerical conversions, and page 5 Example 4 demonstrates the corresponding pronumeral forms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly convert six logarithmic statements to exponential form, including negative and fractional exponents and pronumerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine two logarithms using the product law, then evaluate when the product is a power of the base.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 states and derives the product law; page 3 supplies the standard result for 1; page 4 demonstrates exact-power evaluation; page 5 Example 5 demonstrates the product law in worked calculations. Parts a–c stop at one logarithm; parts d–f also evaluate exactly.
questions.methodNote: Use Logarithmic Law 1 to combine a sum into the logarithm of a product. Evaluate exact powers using the logarithm definition and use log_a 1 = 0.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine two logarithms using the product law, then evaluate when the product is a power of the base.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the quotient law to two logarithms with a common base, then evaluate standard logarithms where possible.

questions.mappingNote: Page 3 states and derives the quotient law and standard results; page 4 demonstrates evaluating reciprocal arguments through negative indices; page 5 Example 5 applies logarithmic laws. Each of parts a–f directly assesses quotient-law simplification.
questions.methodNote: Use logarithmic law 2 to combine a difference as the logarithm of a quotient. Simplify the quotient and use standard logarithmic results or negative indices where applicable.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the quotient law to two logarithms with a common base, then evaluate standard logarithms where possible.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine logarithms using product, quotient and power laws.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly simplify combinations of logarithms using the laws established on pages 2–3.
questions.methodNote: Use product, quotient and power laws, then log of 1 equals 0 where applicable.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine logarithms using product, quotient and power laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Factor arguments into the supplied bases, apply product and power laws and substitute symbols; the final part reverses the product law to recognise log base 10 of 10.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–g extend Example 5 to four supplied logarithms; h combines the given logarithms and uses log base 10 of 10.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 factors arguments, expands products and powers into logarithms, and substitutes the given Greek-letter values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factor arguments and apply log laws to express results in supplied symbolic logarithms.

classification.difficultyReason: Select power, product and quotient laws to consolidate logarithms, then remove logarithms using equal arguments or exponential conversion and rearrange.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires a relation without logarithms; the conversion definition and Example 3 support the final conversion.
questions.methodNote: Apply product, quotient and power laws, then use the equivalence between logarithmic and index form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine logarithms and convert to equivalent algebraic or exponential relations.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand the logarithm of a formula using product and power laws.

questions.mappingNote: The sphere formula supplies a constant factor and a cubic power, directly assessed by logarithmic laws 1 and 3.
questions.methodNote: Take logarithms and expand using the product and power laws.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand the logarithm of a formula using product and power laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Isolate the exponential factor, convert the symbolic equation to logarithmic form and divide by the coefficient of x.

questions.mappingNote: The symbolic conversion demonstrated in Example 4 applies to the isolated equation with exponent bx.
questions.methodNote: Use the index–logarithm equivalence after isolating the exponential expression, then rearrange algebraically.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Isolate an exponential term, take logarithms and rearrange for its exponent variable.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine logarithms into a quotient and convert to exponential form to isolate A.

questions.methodNote: Use the quotient law and the defining conversion between logarithmic and exponential forms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine logarithms into a quotient and convert to exponential form to isolate A.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the specified new base in the change-of-base formula and evaluate the resulting logarithms as integer exponents.

questions.mappingNote: Part a changes to base 3 and part b to base 2, directly matching Example 6 on PDF page 8. The catalogue skill log-results explicitly includes change of base.
questions.methodNote: Use the change-of-base formula, evaluate the numerator and denominator in the specified base, and simplify exactly. Example 6 also checks the result by exponentiation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply change of base to specified integer bases and evaluate logarithms of exact powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute each argument and base into the explicitly requested base-10 quotient, evaluate and round to four decimal places.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess the change-of-base rule included in log-results; no equation solving or further logarithm-law manipulation is required.
questions.methodNote: Apply the change-of-base formula using base 10 logarithms, retain the exact logarithm quotient until calculator evaluation, and round to four decimal places, as demonstrated in Example 7 on PDF page 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of change of base followed by calculator evaluation to the specified precision.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert an exponential equation into a logarithm, evaluate by change of base and account for the negative coefficient of x in the final parts.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly apply Example 8. Parts e and f additionally require isolating x from a negative exponent. Solving exponential equations with logarithms is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 8 converts the exponential equation to logarithmic form, changes to base 10 and rounds the result to four decimal places. Pages 7–8 establish the change-of-base formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert exponential equations to logarithmic form and use change of base, including negative exponents.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply logarithms to exponential equations, including variable exponents on both sides, then solve linear equations.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts extend the taught logarithmic method to exponential equations; parts c and d require collecting variable terms after applying the power law.
questions.methodNote: Pages 7–8 establish change of base and the logarithm power law. Page 9 Example 8 solves an exponential equation using base 10 logarithms, retaining exact logarithmic expressions until four-decimal-place evaluation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply logarithms to exponential equations, including variable exponents on both sides, then solve linear equations.

classification.difficultyReason: Use change of base to simplify products with different logarithmic bases.

questions.mappingNote: Page 8 states both change-of-base forms; pages 8–9 demonstrate changing bases and simplifying exact logarithmic expressions. Question 5 directly assesses these standard results.
questions.methodNote: Use the change-of-base quotient and product formulas, then cancel nonzero logarithmic factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use change of base to simplify products with different logarithmic bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite radicals as powers, change to the specified base a and simplify exponent ratios; the final expression repeats this process before adding the results.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess change of base or its base-a simplification. The closest primary catalogue skill is log-results; logarithm laws and fractional indices support the calculations.
questions.methodNote: Use the change-of-base formula established on pages 7–8 and Example 9 on page 9: change to base a, apply the power law and use log_a a=1. Express radicals as fractional powers before simplifying.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply change of base and the power law, including fractional indices and a sum of three logarithms.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct exponential reference points and apply the taught inverse reflection, swapping coordinates and translating the horizontal asymptote into a vertical one.

questions.methodNote: Page 10 introduces exponential features. Page 11 derives coordinate interchange and reflection in y=x for exponential and logarithmic inverse graphs. Page 12 Example 10 explicitly draws the exponential first, then reflects it in y=x to obtain the logarithmic graph. Page 13 supplies the assigned question and its Example 10 reference.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two logarithmic graphs by reflecting their exponential inverses in the line y=x, as demonstrated in Example 10.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert to x equal to a power of the base, calculate x for the supplied y-values and use the coordinates and asymptote to draw each logarithmic curve.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess table construction and logarithmic graphing. Converting y=log_a(x) to x=a^y supplies the requested five abscissae.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret vertical shifts, scaling and exponent sign changes to place related curves correctly; fractional bases require tracking reciprocal powers and increasing versus decreasing behaviour.

questions.mappingNote: Part a assesses vertical translation, part b vertical scaling, part c reflection in the y-axis, and part d fractional-base graphing with reflection. Exponential transformations is the closest supplied primary skill. Method compatibility for a, b and d remains unresolved.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare logarithmic curves on both sides of x=1, then use a base relationship or vertical scaling to add the base-4 curve without a new value table.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess graphing and comparing logarithmic functions. The printed Example 11 reference is retained, although Example 12 is the directly relevant comparison example.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a doubling model and use logarithms to determine the elapsed time.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a doubling model and use logarithms to determine the elapsed time.

classification.difficultyReason: Build the growth model, solve target-time equations with logarithms, convert mass and time units and explain why the Earth-mass prediction exceeds the model's realistic assumptions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d directly apply the bacterial-growth model and logarithmic time-solving method from Example 13. Part d additionally requires kilograms-to-grams conversion; part e interprets the limitations of sustained exponential growth.
questions.methodNote: Example 13 models bacterial growth using initial amount multiplied by a growth factor raised to elapsed time, then takes base-10 logarithms to solve for time. Examples 14 and 15 reinforce isolating the exponential term and applying the logarithm power law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct an exponential growth model, solve for elapsed time using logarithms, convert mass units and discuss the model's limitations.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct a population model using a calendar-year exponent, substitute a future year and solve a growth equation using logarithms.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses constructing and analysing a population growth model; logarithmic equation solving is required in part c. The calendar year requires the elapsed-time exponent t−1976.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a population model using a calendar-year exponent, substitute a future year and solve a growth equation using logarithms.

classification.difficultyReason: Build two exponential models with different starting years, align their time offsets to solve for a target population ratio, and explain why extrapolating the models beyond equality would make China’s population exceed the world’s.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 applies the growth-model method to calendar-year exponents and compares two populations by equating their exponential models. Population modelling is the closest catalogue match and the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 13 constructs an exponential growth model and solves for elapsed time by isolating the exponential, taking common logarithms and using the power law. Example 14 applies logarithms to a decay model. Example 15 reinforces logarithmic solution of an exponential model.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct and compare exponential population models with different initial years, solve using logarithms, and discuss model limitations.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine a decay constant from two masses, then use logarithms to calculate the half-life.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine a decay constant from two masses, then use logarithms to calculate the half-life.
